title: Entropy-driven quantile batcher — sketch for token-vs-request fairness & KV consistency
body:
TL;DR:
Small sketch for a scheduler variant that balances token-level efficiency and request-level fairness by using an entropy-weighted quantile score. Intended as a middle ground: better tail fairness than pure token-first batching, while preserving kernel-friendly coalescing and KV cache affinity. Draft, lots of open questions and concrete experiments below.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Continuous batching in our runtime is dominated by token-first heuristics: merge tokens aggressively to hit GPU throughput but this can starve short/latency-sensitive requests or high-priority customers.
- Request-level fairness approaches keep per-request latency predictable but sacrifice batch utilization (more small batches, poorer kernel efficiency and reduced KV cache hits).
- KV cache introduces a second axis: coalescing requests with shared prefixes massively reduces work. We need a scheduler that reasons about both token aggregation and KV affinity.
- Kernels have non-linear behavior w.r.t batch size and sequence length distribution (some kernels prefer many short sequences, others long; quantized kernels have different sweet spots).

Goals (non-exhaustive):
- Improve p95 latency for tiered customers while keeping p50 token cost within 5% of current token-first baseline.
- Avoid pathological starvation of small requests.
- Maintain or improve KV cache hit-rate for realistic workloads (goal: +5% hit-rate vs naive request-first).
- Produce a scheduler that is simple enough to reason about and instrument in the runtime.

High-level idea:
- Compute an urgency score for each pending request = alpha * request_priority + beta * deadline_shock + gamma * entropy_penalty.
- Entropy_penalty measures how much mixing this request into a candidate batch would increase token-heterogeneity (and therefore decrease kernel efficiency / KV affinity). Higher entropy => higher penalty.
- Use quantile aggregation: choose a target quantile q (e.g., 0.6) of pending requests by urgency, then attempt to form a batch by greedily adding requests that do not push the batch's entropy / kernel mismatch beyond a threshold. If the batch is below the kernel-sweet-spot, allow speculative waiting with capped latency.

Definitions (working):
- token_count(r): estimated output tokens for request r (prompt + expected gen).
- prefix_key(r): KV cache key or fingerprint for request r's prefix.
- kernel_profile(b): predicted kernel throughput for a batch b (depends on seq length distribution & quantization). We approximate with a small parametric model we already keep for each model variant.
- entropy(B) = - sum_p p_i * log(p_i) where p_i is fraction of tokens in batch from prefix group i (simple grouping by prefix_key hash bucket).
- combined_score(r) = w1 * priority_norm(r) + w2 * (deadline_time_remaining_norm) - w3 * delta_entropy_if_added(r, B) - w4 * kernel_mismatch_penalty_if_added(r, B)
  - all terms normalized to [0,1].

Why entropy?
- We observed experimentally that mixing many distinct prefixes increases memory pressure (KV cache unused) and kernel dispatch inefficiency. Entropy provides a continuous, differentiable-ish proxy instead of discrete affinity heuristics.

Scheduler pseudocode (sketch):
- loop: when GPU can accept a batch or when earliest_deadline crosses threshold:
  1. gather candidate queue Q of pending requests sorted by combined_score descending.
  2. pick q = quantile(Q, q_target). Let seed_set = requests with score >= q.
  3. initialize B = seed_set (or the head k requests, cap by token_count). Compute kernel_profile(B) and entropy(B).
  4. while kernel_profile(B) < kernel_sweet_spot and total_tokens(B) < max_tokens:
     - from remaining Q, choose r that maximizes (score(r) - lambda * delta_entropy_if_added(r,B) - mu * kernel_mismatch_penalty_if_added(r,B)) / token_count(r)
     - if adding r keeps entropy(B) <= entropy_threshold_for_curr_kernel and latency_constraints satisfied, add r to B; else mark r skip_for_this_round.
  5. if B meets min_efficiency or earliest_deadline_exceeded: dispatch B to GPU; else wait up to spec_wait_ms and retry.

Key knobs to expose in config:
- q_target (quantile for admission) e.g., 0.5—0.9
- entropy_threshold per kernel/model variant
- kernel_sweet_spot (expected throughput target in tokens/sec)
- spec_wait_ms (maximum speculative hold before forced dispatch)
- weights w1..w4 (priority/deadline/entropy/kernel mismatch)
- starvation_protection_period per customer (if request waits > X ms, escalate score)

Fairness metrics (proposed):
- request_fairness_index = variance of (observed_latency / SLA_latency) across customers (lower better).
- token_fairness_index = distributional fairness over tokens served per tenant in a window (we don't want one tenant to consume > X% of token throughput unfairly).
- mixed_fairness = weighted combination: alpha * request_fairness + (1-alpha) * token_fairness. Tune alpha in experiments.

KV cache considerations:
- Treat same prefix_key as strong affinity: delta_entropy_if_added for same-prefix is strongly negative (reward).
- But over-rewarding same-prefix creates head-of-line blocking for diversified workloads. Use diminishing returns: the marginal gain from adding the nth request with same prefix decays. Simple formula: kv_bonus = kv_base * (1 - e^{-n/kv_decay}).
- Need to handle tiny prefixes (one-shot user prompts) that should not block entire batch. Add a cap on per-prefix share in a batch (e.g., <= 70% of tokens).

Kernel matching and model variants:
- Maintain lightweight kernel profiles for each model+quantization variant: throughput(token_len_mean, token_len_variance, batch_token_count). We already have telemetry; use moving-window regression to update.
- kernel_mismatch_penalty_if_added = expected drop in throughput (normalized) caused by increasing variance or shifting mean length away from kernel sweet spot.
- Prefer cheaper kernels when mixed batch still meets latency SLOs, otherwise fallback to higher-throughput kernels.

Instrumentation and observability plan:
- Per-batch metadata: seed_quantile, entropy_pre_post, kernel_variant, token_count, expected_throughput, observed_throughput, per-request wait_ms, prefix_bucket_counts.
- Dashboards: p50/p95 latency by weight class, KV hit rate, entropy distribution, effective batch utilization (tokens/ideal_tokens).
- Housekeeping: log sample of decisions for offline RL training later.

Experiments (short list):
1) Microbench synthetic workload: mix of (a) many short single-token requests (b) long 1024-token generations (c) prefix-shared groups of size 10, 50. Measure p50/p95, KV hit-rate, and GPU utilization. Compare: token-first baseline, request-first baseline, and this entropy-quantile approach across q_target grid.
2) Real traffic A/B with small percent of traffic from hosted API (non-enterprise customers) to validate p95 improvements and no regression on cost per token.
3) Kernel-sensitivity sweep: run same workloads against quantized and non-quant kernels to see where entropy penalty should be steeper.

Rollout and gating:
- Start as an opt-in policy behind feature flag on a subset of pods.
- Gate 1: no regression in p50 tokens cost >5%. Gate 2: p95 latency improvement for priority buckets >10% or non-regression. Gate 3: KV hit-rate non-degradation.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to tune q_target automatically based on current queue shape? Quick idea: set q_target = CDF^{-1}(utilization_target) where utilization_target derived from throughput budget. Need experiments.
- Is entropy the best continuous proxy for affinity? Alternatives: similarity embeddings of prefixes (expensive); hashed-group counts (discrete).
- Interaction with rate-limiter and quotas: should heavy tenants be penalized by lower combined_score or handled by separate admission controller?
- Cold-start behavior for kernels with little telemetry: default conservative params or fallback to token-first?
- Formal fairness guarantees? This sketch uses heuristics; consider proving bounded waiting time per request class.

Implementation notes / integration with runtime:
- This scheduler can be implemented as a pluggable admission policy in batcher_manager.go. Keep computation O(n log n) for queue length n with incremental entropy updates for O(1) per add.
- Need to augment request metadata with prefix_key fingerprint and tenant_priority on entry.
- Export small kernel_profile API: PredictThroughput(model, variant, mean_len, var_len, tokens) -> tokens/sec. Precompute for common buckets.
- Add unit tests for edge cases: all identical prefixes (should yield low entropy), all distinct (high entropy).

Notes to self:
- Talk to Arjun about telemetry fields to see if we have per-request prefix fingerprint already.
- Lina to prototype entropy delta computation in python using current trace logs.
- Carlos to run synthetic bench matrix on a single c5g/gpu node.

References / related drafts (internal):
- request-token-harmony-orchestrator-sketch.json (conceptual overlap, but that doc focuses on ledger-based fairness)
- kv-affinity-playbook.md (older notes about grouping by prefix)
- runtime PR #4123 (experimental throughput model)

Bottom line:
This is an exploratory middle ground — entropy gives a compact signal to trade off KV affinity and mixing. The quantile admission idea lets us prioritize urgent requests but still protect kernel efficiency. If experiments show promise we can refine the math and expose a small set of knobs for SRE/Product to tune per-customer SLAs.

Unresolved: set concrete defaults for weights w1..w4 and q_target; need data-driven choices.
